title: El gobierno de Venezuela y la represión sin castigo desde el 2014
content: According to the UN Independent Mission on Venezuela, repression has continued without punishment from July 2024 to August 2025. The report documents 25 deaths, 2,220 detentions, 218 children detained, 200 detentions recorded between January and August 2025, and 84 foreign detainees. It also reports 200 detentions in the period, including 84 on 10 January and 42 on 25 May, and 74 between the two events. The mission notes that 26 detainees were held incommunicado for weeks or months, and that 7 cases of torture involved denial of food, water, and medical care. The report states that 22 cases of gender‑based violence were documented, and that 18 journalists were detained, with 11 still in custody. The mission estimates 120–150 foreign detainees, of whom 84 have been documented. The report claims that 6 of 14 deaths examined were attributable to the government, with 6 others pointing in that direction. The mission also cites that "El número creciente de manifestaciones populares contra los resultados anunciados por el Consejo Nacional Electoral desataron un proceso de detenciones masivas" (the growing number of popular demonstrations triggered a mass detention process).

title: Venezuela: La persecución por motivos políticos se está intensificando, advierte la Misión Independiente
content: The United Nations Independent Mission on the Determination of Facts (UNIM) released a report to the UN Human Rights Council warning that political persecution in Venezuela is escalating. The mission documented that in the protests that followed the July 28, 2024 presidential election, 25 people were killed between July 29 and 30, with security forces involved in at least 12 of those deaths. In Maracay, members of the National Bolivarian Guard and the army fired on demonstrators, killing six; the report notes that ‘a victim was shot with a shotgun at less than 10 metres’. The mission also recorded five deaths of detainees during protests in 2024 and 2025, and identified ‘reasonable grounds to believe that the state did not provide timely medical care’, subjecting detainees to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. In 2024, 2,220 people were detained, of whom 200 were released progressively, yet the mission recorded at least 200 new selective detentions of government critics in 2025. Alarmingly, 220 children aged 13‑17 were detained, subjected to isolation, sexual violence and violations of due process, with four adolescents still held in La Guaira and Lara. The mission’s experts, including Marta Valiñas, Patricia Tappatá and Francisco Cox, stated that ‘the Fiscalía has not reported progress in investigations, and all deaths remain in impunity’, and that ‘detentions of 2025 repeat the pattern of 2024: without legal basis, carried out by masked individuals and with fabricated criminal files’. The report describes systematic torture methods such as asphyxiation with plastic bags, beatings, electric shocks to genitalia and rape threats, and notes that laws on ‘NGO financing’ and ‘Simón Bolívar’ have been used to suppress civil society. Valiñas concluded that ‘the evidence confirms that the crime of political persecution continues in Venezuela, with no national authority showing willingness to prevent, prosecute or punish these grave human‑rights violations’. The mission’s findings highlight that Venezuela’s justice system has abdicated its role, leaving the international community as the last hope for victims.

title: Venezuela: U.N. report alleges pattern of reprisals against opponents
content: A U.N. Fact‑Finding Mission report released on Sept. 23, 2025 documents a "sustained and systematic pattern" of political persecution in Venezuela, including the detention of relatives of opposition figures to create a climate of fear. The report cites new evidence of harsh post‑election repression after the July 28, 2024 presidential vote, when the National Electoral Council declared Nicolás Maduro the winner without publishing tally sheets. It records 25 deaths and more than 2,220 detentions, including at least 218 children and adolescents, and between 120 and 150 foreign nationals accused of mercenary or terrorist activities. Detainees began to be released on Nov. 15, 2024; by March, official data from the Public Ministry reported 2,006 releases, while the rights group Foro Penal recorded only 1,399 (1,209 men and 190 women). The mission documented 18 cases of journalists detained between August 2024 and August 2025, targeting them as government opponents. In five previous reports since 2020, the mission made at least 145 recommendations to the Venezuelan state, none of which were implemented, allowing repression to deepen. Edmundo González, recognized internationally as the legitimate winner of the July 28 election, wrote on X: 'There are truths that admit no discussion. In the face of torture, sexual violence, forced disappearance or death, there can be no compromise or justification.' He added, 'This report points to clear responsibility before the international community. The voices expressed today at the Human Rights Council are a necessary step, but insufficient given the magnitude of what has been confirmed. Venezuela needs the active and sustained solidarity of democratic nations.' On the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, González and opposition leader María Corina Machado called for international support of Venezuela’s "popular sovereignty" and urged the dismantling of Maduro’s regime and prosecution of those who "violate" the law and human rights. Machado said, 'Venezuela will move forward in an orderly and peaceful democratic transition.... You can count on the brave people of Venezuela to carry out this historic task, and we are counting on you.'

title: Asfixias y descargas eléctricas: así torturaron a 220 adolescentes detenidos en protestas
content: The United Nations Mission on the Determination of Facts (UN-MDF) released a report detailing the arbitrary detention and torture of at least 220 Venezuelan minors during post‑election protests. Between 29 July and 30 August 2024, and again on 10 January 2025, the report records 187 male, 22 female and 11 unidentified minors aged 12‑17 were arrested, with 4 still in custody. Carabobo state had the highest number of documented cases. The UN report notes that most arrests occurred in public spaces during protests, but also that minors were detained while waiting for public transport, leaving medical appointments or playing football. One testimony describes a group threatening a voter with the phrase: 'Esa sonrisita se te va a quitar pronto', and the next day a 15‑year‑old son was arrested while playing in the street. The mission documented that many minors were used as retaliation against family members or political opponents, and that armed, masked operatives entered homes to detain children. In Amazonas, Anzoátegui and Zulia, children as young as 13 were held for hours or days without charges, violating Venezuela’s Law for the Protection of Children, Adolescents and Youth (Lopnna). The UN report highlights that the detention pattern mirrored that used for adults: no warrants, no communication with families, and processing as adults. Detentions were marked by delayed hearings beyond the 48‑hour legal limit, lack of legal representation, and accusations of terrorism or incitement to hatred without evidence. In at least one case, a judge attempted to coerce minors into pleading guilty for reduced sentences. The mission also warned of sexual or gender‑based abuses during detention. Torture methods included beatings, death threats, asphyxiation with plastic bags, and electric shocks. In Carabobo, a 16‑year‑old was taken to a military facility where he was beaten with a bat, asphyxiated and subjected to electric shocks to force a confession. Another 16‑year‑old with autism was similarly asphyxiated and shocked on 2 August 2024. Psychological effects reported among released minors include post‑traumatic stress, anxiety, sleep disturbances, social isolation and violent episodes; families suffered depression, emotional exhaustion and health problems due to lack of communication. Of the 220 cases, 216 minors were released under precautionary measures deemed harsher than those applied to adults, requiring them to appear before Caracas courts every eight days. Four minors remain in prison: three in La Guaira and one in Lara. The UN mission held judges in several regions accountable for approving these irregularities and warned that protests in Venezuela are suppressed not only through arbitrary detentions but through a systematic pattern of torture and violations of due process that severely affect children and adolescents.

title: Venezuela: Reporte periódico de monitoreo (1 de enero - 30 junio 2025) - Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)
content:
In the first half of 2025, Venezuela’s humanitarian response reached 1.5 million people, of whom 58 % were women and girls, representing 29 % of the estimated target population of 5.1 million. The actions were carried out in 285 municipalities across 24 states, with the collaboration of 110 national and international humanitarian organisations, the Red Cross movement and United Nations agencies, coordinated with authorities. The clusters with the greatest reach were Food Security and Livelihoods, Health, Nutrition and Water, and Sanitation and Hygiene (ASH). 

Funding remained limited: by 30 June, donors had contributed US$58 million, which is 8.4 % of the US$606.5 million required for the year, the lowest level since the establishment of the Humanitarian Response Plan (PRH). Despite this, implementing partners maintained a coverage level similar to the previous year, largely because many first‑semester activities were financed by 2024 funds and because organisations adapted their implementation modes, prioritising actions that sustain population reach through counselling, training and continuous resource optimisation. 

Key sectors—health, water, sanitation and hygiene, protection, nutrition and food security—experienced significant reductions in specialised and individualised services, disproportionately affecting children, women and vulnerable communities. The lack of resources threatens the continuity of essential services and underscores the urgent need for new funding to prevent further deterioration in coverage and the ability to maintain adequate standards of humanitarian response. 

The response continued to focus on localisation, with 58 % of PRH implementing partners being national and local organisations, a factor critical for ensuring access to vulnerable communities and strengthening local capacities.

title: Libertad de expresión en Venezuela: 89 violaciones en lo que va de 2025 - Runrun.es: En defensa de tus derechos humanos
content: The NGO Espacio Público reported 89 cases of violations of freedom of expression in Venezuela, amounting to 167 complaints. The most frequent violations were censorship and intimidation, each with 48 incidents, followed by administrative restriction (24), judicial harassment (23), verbal harassment (13), and threats (11). The number of cases fell 64 % compared with the same period last year, and the number of violations fell 67 %, yet the NGO warned that this decline does not signal structural improvement, citing the large‑scale state repression that marked 2024 before, during, and after the presidential elections. Journalists and reporters were the most affected group, with 30 victims (≈35 % of all victims). They were followed by private individuals (15 victims), media outlets (12 victims), and web platforms (12 victims), together accounting for 75 % of all victims. Regarding perpetrators, state institutions led with 57 incidents (45 % of all), followed closely by security forces (35 incidents, 28 %) and private operators (24 incidents, 19 %). 'Esta disminución no indica una mejora estructural, ya que el 2024 estuvo marcado por una represión estatal a gran escala, antes, durante y después de las elecciones presidenciales', the NGO stated.

title: Utopix registró 76 feminicidios en el primer semestre de 2025
content: During the first half of 2025, Utopix recorded 15 confirmed feminicides in Venezuela, bringing the annual total to 76. The NGO’s monthly monitoring, based on media and social‑media reports, stresses the need for a Feminist Emergency Plan. In 2025 a feminicide occurred every 57 hours and a femicide in the ‘frustration’ category every 44 hours, compared with one every 34 hours at the 2020 peak. In June, Aragua had the most cases (3), followed by Apure, Miranda and Barinas (2 each). Victims were mostly aged 26‑40, with a peak at 56‑60. Weapon use: 7 firearms, 4 knives, 1 blunt force, 1 asphyxiation, 1 gynecobstetric violence, 1 vehicle. Seven bodies were left on the street, three mutilated, two tortured, one sexually abused, one staged accident. Of 19 perpetrators identified, 8 were arrested, 3 fugitives, 3 suicides, 1 died in a police encounter, 2 had criminal records, 4 unknown. Five victims were mothers, one pregnant, and at least two children were left orphaned. Four families reported prior abuse. Of the 19, 8 were intimate partners, 2 gang‑related, 1 family member, 1 non‑intimate, 1 vicario, 1 gynecobstetric, 1 unknown. Utopix also logged 16 femicides of Venezuelan women abroad in Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, Chile, Spain, Colombia and Ecuador. The report highlights ongoing structural impunity and calls for urgent state action. 'Es imperativo visibilizar estos casos y exigir al Estado acciones urgentes para enfrentar la violencia de género', said the investigators.

title: Estados de emergência reforçam repressão e controlo social na Venezuela
content: The Venezuelan Program for Education and Human Rights Action (Provea), a non-governmental organization, warned of the 'chronic abuse' of states of emergency in Venezuela, stating they have been used to increase repression and social control. Between 2015 and 2025, over 12 decrees of exceptional state were issued by President Nicolás Maduro’s government. In 2015, eight states of exception were declared in 26 municipalities across four border states, citing paramilitarism, drug trafficking, and illegal mining, leading to the criminalization and stigmatization of hundreds of border residents as smugglers and traitors. In Zúlia, military presence in La Guajira intensified, resulting in abuses against Indigenous Wayúu and Añú communities. Provea reported that military personnel were accused of over 19 killings of Indigenous people, dozens of torture cases, inhumane treatment, hundreds of arbitrary detentions, and illegal home invasions. These measures supported the 'Operations of People's Liberation,' which caused the forced displacement of over 20,000 people from Táchira to Colombia due to military and police violence. In 2016, a continuous and unconstitutional economic state of emergency was imposed, suspending the powers of Venezuela’s National Assembly and labeling its functions as threats to national security. This prolonged state of exception created a parallel legal framework, indefinitely suspending constitutional rights such as freedom of association, assembly, expression, information, and peaceful protest, subordinating citizens' rights to state interests and national security. In 2017, Maduro established the Special Actions Forces (FAES) under similar justifications, and in 2018, a decree extended the economic emergency, erasing the distinction between national defense and citizen security, and increasing FAES lethality. Provea documented hundreds of FAES abuses, including extrajudicial executions and illegal invasions. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a state of alarm was declared, enabling the 'Bolivarian Fury' campaign, which intensified arbitrary arrests and persecution of social and political activists. Provea emphasized that none of these decrees met constitutional principles of proportionality and temporal limits, instead being used to expand political repression and social control under the guise of national security. The current 'state of external commotion' (emergency), declared on September 29, 2025, by Maduro in response to alleged U.S. threats, has raised deep concern, as it may signal a step toward total militarization and increased human rights violations. Tensions between Caracas and Washington escalated in August after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered warships to the Caribbean, citing the fight against Latin American drug cartels.

title: ¿Normalidad democrática en Venezuela? Informe revela la profundización del autoritarismo, la represión y el miedo
content: The human‑rights report *27J: La Normalización Fallida* documents a deepening of authoritarianism in Venezuela for the period June‑August 2025. It records 1,056 political prisoners by September 2025, including 41 foreigners and 48 binational detainees, who are used as "fichas de negociación" or "diplomacia de rehenes". The municipal elections of 27 July were a "simulacro" with only 29 % turnout, the lowest ever for municipal polls, yet the ruling party won 85 % of the mayoralties. The report cites that 24 % of the world’s cocaine transit passed through Venezuela in 2023, generating more than US$8.185 million in 2024, and that high‑ranking civil and military officials are allegedly linked to the Cartel de los Soles. 167 violations of freedom of expression were documented between January and August 2025, including 24 detentions of journalists. 71 arbitrary detentions were recorded in the same period, 63 % of them against party militants, and 45 % of those involved short‑term forced disappearances. 6.87 million Venezuelans were displaced across 17 Latin American countries by mid‑2025, with more than 14,000 forced to return south from the U.S. and Mexico. In the EU, 49,000 Venezuelans applied for asylum in the first half of 2025, but only 0.02 % were granted refugee status. The report concludes that these patterns—simulation of elections, state capture by illicit economies, suppression of civic space, systematic detentions and forced disappearances—constitute crimes of humanity and calls for continued international pressure.

title: 83% de los venezolanos están dispuestos a defender el país en una eventual agresión - Agencia Venezolana de Noticias
content: According to a national survey conducted by the polling firm Hinterlaces on October 8, 2025, 83% of Venezuelans stated they would be willing to defend the country in the event of a foreign military invasion. Only 6% said they would not, and 11% chose not to respond. The survey, which included 1,200 interviews nationwide with a margin of error of ±3%, reflects a strong patriotic sentiment and national unity that transcends political differences. Regarding motivations for a potential foreign intervention, 89% of respondents believed the true goal would be to overthrow President Nicolás Maduro and seize Venezuela’s oil resources, while only 6% thought military action could be justified on the grounds of combating drug trafficking. The findings indicate that the majority of Venezuelans perceive external aggression as driven by economic and geopolitical interests rather than humanitarian concerns, reinforcing their commitment to resist and defend national sovereignty.
